subject: Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization

messages.author: 8c4f70ab584cd6d9
messages.subject: Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
parts:
My sense is that when using groups Stan likely spends a lot of time in loops when there are opportunities to use vectorization.

In the attached code, I created an unbalanced panel of about 190,000 observations. I allow the mean to vary between five groups. In the original Stan regression, I use a loop and effectively a lookup to get the correct mean to use. In the alternate method, I split the data up before I put it into Stan, so that I can take advantage of vectorization better.

In one run, the original method takes 320.8s on my work machine (4 chains, average: 80.2s), while the alternate method takes 67.4s (4 chains, average 16.9s). So it gave a nearly 5x speed up. As this is just one simple test, I'm not sure how much this is influenced by the number of groups or their size.

To me, the biggest downside to this approach is that it is much less flexible. It requires splitting up data and hard-coding the different groups in the Stan file. This suggests that maybe there is scope for improvements to the Stan language to facilitate this type of data (and so that Stan can recognize it and adjust things properly to take into account the vectorization).

For instance, in my approach, I am doing the regression with centered data because I didn't feel like putting in individual-level intercepts for the purpose of demonstrating this. The individual-level intercept version runs significantly slower (I believe it is more accurate, but I'm a little worried by it since the intercept is correlated with the group means). However, if Stan could, on its end, split up the data into the relevant groups and then just apply the correct normal vector sum to each, then I think it could be much faster.

I don't recall seeing this as a recommended strategy anywhere to speed up Stan code. I can put in a Github issue if this is original.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
parts:
I don't understand what the models are supposed to do.
It looks like ff_alt.stan is fitting five intercept-only
linear regressions for y_1 through y_5 that share the error
scale sigma_e. And there's no use of N_obs --- was that
on purpose?

The loops per se aren't what's slow, it's the result of
how they construct the expression graph through which Stan
propagates the chain rule to compute derivatives. Vectorization
lets us collapse this graph and reuse shared expressions.

And yes, we do talk about aggregating data if sufficient
statistics are available in the optimization chapter of the
manual.

- Bob

messages.author: 8c4f70ab584cd6d9
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
parts:
The files are merely to demonstrate the difference in performance. Not an actual application. But yes, the idea is to fit an intercept-only model with different intercepts for the groups but with the same standard deviation. The ff.stan file should produce similar results as the ff_alt.stan file, but with a different implementation. ff.stan fits a different mean to each of the groups with the same error, while ff_alt.stan splits the data up into separate inputs before putting the data in stan.

The N_obs variable is in ff.stan, but in ff_alt.stan there is a separate one for each of the inputs because it is an unbalanced panel and not all of them are the same length. I guess what's not used in ff_alt.stan is N, not N_obs. That's just some extra stuff that got carried over (for instance the ff.stan file also has a tt variable that is superfluous, the result of changes I had made to simplify it and didn't entirely clean up, sorry).

With respect to your point about collapsing the expression graph, I was just speculating as to my point about loops.

With respect to aggregating data, I see a sub-section on exploiting sufficient statistics. I had seen that example, but assumed that it was really just another approach to vectorization. I don't really know what exploiting sufficient statistics means and it isn't explained in the manual beyond saying "hey this is a thing". I googled it and the wikipedia page on sufficient statistics has a section on the normal distribution. Maybe my approach is similar to that...but I would have never thought that this idea was in the manual. Anyway, I don't consider this approach like aggregating data. Maybe more like de-aggregating data (or manually de-grouping hierarchical data).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
parts:
I believe in the example you sent you could go a step
further by using the sufficient stats for the normal to
compute the posterior analytically. A sufficient stat is
just a summary stat of data that is enough information for
estimtion. It only works in exponential families.

But even the aggregation you're doing will help, as you
saw. Basically anything that gets the data into a
vectorized form to reduce the expression graph size and
reduce redundant calculations will help.

I'll add a note to that effect in the manual. I'm not sure
what you meant by adding a GitHub issue --- were you thinking
we could somehow automate this, or was it just about the doc? If
it's just about the doc, I added the note here for the next manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617#issuecomment-156593302

Thanks.

- Bob

P.S. We have an arXiv paper that goes into the gory details of
the autodiff if you're interested --- that's where all the
purely computational efficiency considerations are (there are
also statistical considerations like fatness of tails and
varying posterior curvature which can motivate reparameterizations).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Splitting Hierarchical Data to Improve Vectorization
parts:
I should add that another aggregation technique that is
useful is to count the number of times a given data point y[i] occurs
N[i] times you can code this as follows:

for (i in 1:I)
increment_log_prob(N[i] * normal_log(y[i], mu, sigma));

This is better than a loop doing them one data point at a time.

- Bob
